decks.title: Chemical Equilibrium — Part 1: Equilibrium, the law of mass action, Kc and Kp
goals: Distinguish reversible and irreversible reactions and explain why physical and chemical equilibria are dynamic
State the law of mass action, write Kc and Kp and their units, and derive Kp = Kc (RT)^Δn
Calculate equilibrium constants and equilibrium amounts, including degree of dissociation, from given data

slides.heading: When does a change stop changing?
slides.body_md: Part 1: **equilibrium** is the state in which nothing seems to change although both directions of change go on. We meet **reversible** reactions, the **law of mass action**, **Kc** and **Kp**.

nodes.label: Law of mass action: Kc and Kp

visual.alt: Flow chart of the topics of Part 1

slides.narration: Welcome to Part One of chemical equilibrium. Many changes do not go to completion, but settle into a state where nothing seems to change, though changes in both directions carry on. We start with reversible reactions and physical equilibria, then learn the law of mass action, the equilibrium constants, and how to calculate with them.

slides.heading: Reversible and irreversible reactions
slides.body_md: An **irreversible** reaction goes (almost) to completion in one direction: magnesium burning in air. A **reversible** reaction can go in both directions, written with **⇌**, and in a **closed vessel** reaches a state in which reactants and products are both present.

rows: Burning of magnesium in air (open dish)
oxide does not return to the metal; products escape
both gases present at all times
ester and water react to give back the acid

visual.alt: Table of irreversible and reversible changes with reasons

slides.narration: An irreversible reaction goes to completion in one direction, like magnesium burning in air. A reversible reaction can go both ways. We write it with a double arrow. In a closed vessel such a reaction reaches a state where both reactants and products are present, and they stop changing in amount.

slides.heading: Liquid and vapour in a sealed flask
slides.body_md: Evaporation starts at a **constant rate**. As vapour builds up, **condensation** speeds up. When the two **rates are equal**, the vapour pressure stays **constant**: a **dynamic equilibrium**. Nothing has stopped; molecules keep crossing the surface both ways.

visual.alt: A sealed flask with liquid and vapour and a graph of the rates of evaporation and condensation reaching equality
visual.caption: Dynamic equilibrium: the two rates are equal, the pressure is constant.

slides.narration: This sealed flask holds a liquid and its vapour. Molecules leave the liquid at a steady rate. As the vapour builds up, more molecules return to the liquid. After some time the rate of leaving equals the rate of returning, the vapour pressure stops changing, and the system is in dynamic equilibrium. Nothing has stopped, both changes go on.

slides.heading: Three kinds of physical equilibrium
slides.body_md: A physical equilibrium involves **changes of state** only. Each is established in a **closed system** at **constant temperature**, and a property stays constant: melting point, vapour pressure.

visual.alt: Table of solid-liquid, liquid-vapour and solid-vapour equilibria

slides.narration: There are three kinds of physical equilibrium. Solid and liquid, such as ice and water at the normal melting point. Liquid and vapour in a closed vessel at a fixed temperature. And solid and vapour, as in iodine or camphor in a closed flask. In each case some property, like the vapour pressure, stays constant.

slides.heading: Quick check: why is the vapour pressure constant?
slides.body_md: Think about both directions of change at the surface of the liquid.
slides.narration: Quick check. Imagine a sealed bottle of ethanol left for a few hours at constant temperature. The vapour pressure stops rising. Decide what is happening at the surface of the liquid at that stage, and choose the explanation that keeps both processes going.

slides.heading: Chemical equilibrium is dynamic
slides.body_md: In a reversible reaction in a **closed system** the **forward rate** falls and the **reverse rate** rises until they are **equal**. Then the concentrations stay constant: the **equilibrium state**. It is **dynamic** because both reactions continue; it can be reached from **either side**; a **catalyst** does not change its position.

rows: nothing enters or leaves; temperature constant
concentrations, pressure and colour no longer change
composition depends on T, not on the route

visual.alt: Table of the characteristics of a chemical equilibrium

slides.narration: In a reversible reaction in a closed vessel the forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they become equal. The concentrations then stay constant. This state is dynamic, because both reactions continue. The same state is reached from either side, and a catalyst only helps the system get there sooner.

slides.heading: Law of mass action and Kc
slides.body_md: The rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the **active masses** (molar concentrations) of the reactants. At equilibrium the two rates are equal, so for **aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD**: $K_c = \dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$. Pure **solids and liquids** do not appear. $K_c$ is constant **at a given temperature**.

visual.alt: Table of equilibrium constant expressions

slides.narration: The law of mass action says that the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the molar concentrations of the reactants. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so the products of concentrations raised to their coefficients, divided by those of reactants, give a constant at a given temperature. Pure solids and liquids are left out.

slides.heading: Worked example: calculating Kc
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** At equilibrium in a closed vessel at 500 K, $[\text{NO}] = 0.20$, $[\text{Cl}_2] = 0.10$ and $[\text{NOCl}] = 0.40$ mol L⁻¹ for $\ce{2NO(g) + Cl2(g) <=> 2NOCl(g)}$ (given). Find $K_c$ with its unit.

$K_c = \dfrac{[\text{NOCl}]^2}{[\text{NO}]^2[\text{Cl}_2]} = \dfrac{(0.40)^2}{(0.20)^2(0.10)} = 40$ L mol⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the calculation of Kc for nitrosyl chloride formation

slides.narration: Write the expression first, with the product concentration squared on top and the reactant concentrations on the bottom. Substituting gives zero point one six divided by zero point zero zero four, which is forty. The unit is litres per mole, because there is one fewer mole of gas on the product side.

slides.heading: Kp, and the units of K
slides.body_md: For gases the equilibrium constant can be written with **partial pressures**: $K_p = \dfrac{p_C^c\,p_D^d}{p_A^a\,p_B^b}$. The unit depends on **Δn = (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants)**: Kc in (mol L⁻¹)^Δn and Kp in (atm)^Δn.

visual.alt: Table of the units of Kc and Kp for four gaseous reactions

slides.narration: For gases we can write the constant with partial pressures, giving Kp. The units of both constants depend on the change in the number of moles of gas. If it is zero there is no unit. If it is plus one, Kc has moles per litre and Kp has atmospheres. If it is negative, the units are inverted.

slides.heading: Derivation: Kp = Kc (RT)^Δn
slides.body_md: For an ideal gas $pV = nRT$, so **p = (n/V) RT = [gas] RT**. Put $p = [\,]RT$ for each gas in $K_p$: the **RT** factors give $(RT)^{(c+d)-(a+b)}$, so **$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$**, with Δn the change in moles of gas.

nodes.label: Replace each p in Kp by [gas] RT

visual.alt: Flow chart of the derivation of Kp equals Kc times RT to the power delta n

slides.narration: Here is the derivation. For an ideal gas the pressure equals the concentration times R T. Replace each partial pressure in the expression for Kp by its concentration times R T. The R T factors collect into R T raised to the number of product moles minus reactant moles. So Kp equals Kc times R T to the power delta n.

slides.heading: Quick check: units of Kp
slides.body_md: First find Δn for the gases, then raise atm to that power.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the moles of gas on each side of the equation, and subtract reactants from products to get delta n. The unit of Kp is atmosphere raised to that number. If the number is negative the unit is inverted, if it is zero there is no unit.

slides.heading: Worked example: Kp from Kc
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{2NO + Cl2 <=> 2NOCl}$ at 500 K, $K_c = 40$ L mol⁻¹. Find $K_p$ ($R = 0.0821$ L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).

$\Delta n = 2 - 3 = -1$, so $K_p = K_c(RT)^{-1} = \dfrac{40}{0.0821 \times 500} = \dfrac{40}{41.05} \approx 0.97$ atm⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the conversion of Kc to Kp for nitrosyl chloride formation

slides.narration: Count the moles of gas. Two on the right and three on the left, so delta n is minus one. The relation then divides Kc by R T. At five hundred kelvin, R T is forty one point oh five, so Kp is about zero point nine seven, with the unit inverse atmospheres.

slides.heading: Quick check: a Kp from partial pressures
slides.body_md: Divide the product of the product pressures by the pressure of the reactant.
slides.narration: Quick check. Write the expression for Kp using partial pressures, with the product pressures multiplied on top and the reactant pressure underneath. Substitute the given pressures in atmospheres and give the answer with its unit.

slides.heading: Characteristics of the equilibrium constant
slides.body_md: **K depends only on temperature.** It does not depend on starting concentrations, pressure or a catalyst. **Reverse the equation: K → 1/K.** **Multiply the equation by n: K → Kⁿ.** **Add equations: multiply their K values.** A large K means products are favoured; a small K means reactants are favoured. Recap from thermodynamics: $\Delta G^\circ = -2.303\,RT\log K$.

rows: Add a catalyst or change pressure

visual.alt: Table of how the equilibrium constant changes when the equation or conditions are altered

slides.narration: The equilibrium constant depends only on temperature. Reverse the equation and the constant is inverted. Double all the coefficients and the constant is squared. When two equations are added, their constants multiply. A large constant means the products are favoured, and a catalyst or a pressure change does not alter its value.

slides.heading: Worked example: equilibrium amounts for an ester
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 1.0 mol of ethanoic acid and 1.0 mol of ethanol are mixed; $K_c = 4.0$ for $\ce{CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O}$. Find the amount of ester at equilibrium.

$K_c = \dfrac{x^2}{(1-x)^2} = 4.0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{x}{1-x} = 2 \Rightarrow x = 0.67$ mol.

visual.alt: ICE table for the esterification of ethanoic acid with ethanol

slides.narration: Set up the initial, change and equilibrium rows. The amount x of ester formed is also the amount of water formed. Since there is no change in the number of moles, the volume cancels. The constant is x squared over one minus x all squared, equal to four. The square root gives two, so x is two thirds of a mole.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Reversible reactions in a closed vessel reach a dynamic equilibrium: equal forward and reverse rates, constant properties.
Physical equilibria: solid–liquid, liquid–vapour, solid–vapour.
Kc = [products]^coeff / [reactants]^coeff; pure solids and liquids are omitted; Kp uses partial pressures.
Kp = Kc (RT)^Δn, with Δn the change in moles of gas.
K depends only on temperature; reverse: 1/K; add equations: multiply K.

visual.alt: Summary table of the key ideas of Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part One. Reversible reactions in closed vessels reach a dynamic equilibrium with equal forward and reverse rates. The constant Kc is built from the concentrations, Kp from the partial pressures, and they are related through R T raised to delta n. Both depend only on temperature.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write the expression from the balanced equation, with coefficients as powers; leave out pure solids and liquids.
In a derivation, start from pV = nRT, give p = [gas]RT, and define Δn.
Use R = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ with atm and litres; temperature in kelvin.
Divide moles by the volume before substituting in Kc unless the volume cancels.
Always state the unit of K, or write "no unit" when Δn = 0.

rows: Forgetting Δn is for gases only

Use the right value of R with the right units, and temperature in kelvin. Divide moles by volume, and always state the unit of the constant.

goals: State Le Chatelier's principle and predict the effect of concentration, temperature, pressure, a catalyst and an inert gas
Explain why a catalyst does not change K or the equilibrium composition
Justify the conditions used for the Haber process, the contact process, the dissociation of N₂O₄ and ester hydrolysis

slides.heading: Pushing an equilibrium
slides.body_md: Part 2: what happens when a system at equilibrium is **disturbed**? **Le Chatelier's principle** predicts the response, and it guides the choice of conditions in industry.

visual.alt: Flow chart of the topics of Part 2

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two. What happens when we disturb a system at equilibrium? Le Chatelier gave a simple rule to predict the response. We apply it to changes of concentration, temperature, pressure, a catalyst and an inert gas, and then use it to choose the best conditions for industrial processes.

slides.heading: Le Chatelier's principle
slides.body_md: If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a **change** of concentration, temperature or pressure, the equilibrium **shifts** in the direction that **opposes** (reduces) the change. It predicts the **direction** of the shift; only a change of **temperature** alters the value of **K**.

visual.alt: Table of disturbances, the direction of shift and the effect on K

slides.narration: The Le Chatelier principle says that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts in the direction that reduces the disturbance. Adding a reactant or removing a product shifts the equilibrium forward. A temperature rise favours the endothermic direction. Only a change of temperature alters the value of the constant.

slides.heading: Effect of concentration
slides.body_md: Adding a reactant makes **Q < K**, so the net reaction goes **forward** until Q = K again; removing a product does the same. Adding a product, or removing a reactant, makes Q > K and shifts the equilibrium **backward**. **K is unchanged.**

visual.alt: Table of the effect of changing concentrations on the iron thiocyanate equilibrium

slides.narration: Adding a reactant makes the reaction quotient smaller than the constant, so the net reaction runs forward until the two are equal again. Removing a product has the same effect. Adding a product, or removing a reactant, pushes the equilibrium backward. The constant itself does not change when concentrations are altered.

slides.heading: Response to added reactant and to compression
slides.body_md: At the first dashed line **N₂O₄ is added**: the equilibrium shifts **forward**. At the second the **volume is halved**: both concentrations double, Q > K, and the system shifts **backward**, towards fewer moles of gas. After each, **Q returns to K**.

visual.alt: Concentrations of N2O4 and NO2 against time when N2O4 is added and then the volume is halved
visual.caption: The system shifts to oppose each disturbance (illustrative kinetic model).

slides.narration: In this model, extra nitrogen tetroxide is added at the first line. Its concentration jumps, and then falls as more nitrogen dioxide forms, the shift forward. At the second line the volume is halved, so both concentrations double at once. The system then shifts back towards nitrogen tetroxide, which has fewer moles of gas.

slides.heading: Quick check: the colour after adding a reactant
slides.body_md: Decide whether Q becomes smaller or larger than K, and which way the net reaction goes.
slides.narration: Quick check. Iron three plus ions and thiocyanate ions make a red complex. If more iron three plus is added, ask whether the quotient becomes smaller or larger than the constant, which way the net reaction then goes, and what that does to the red colour.

slides.heading: Effect of temperature
slides.body_md: Heat behaves like a **reactant** in an endothermic reaction and like a **product** in an exothermic one. **Raising T** favours the **endothermic** direction and **K changes**: it increases for an endothermic and decreases for an exothermic reaction. Lowering T does the opposite.

visual.alt: Table of the effect of a temperature rise on four equilibria

slides.narration: Heat can be thought of as a reactant in an endothermic reaction and a product in an exothermic one. Raising the temperature therefore favours the endothermic direction. This is the only change that alters the value of the equilibrium constant: it increases for an endothermic reaction and decreases for an exothermic one.

slides.heading: Effect of pressure
slides.body_md: Compressing a gas mixture favours the side with **fewer moles of gas**; lowering the pressure favours the side with **more**. If **Δn = 0**, there is **no shift**. Solids and liquids hardly respond. K is unchanged.

visual.alt: Table of the effect of pressure on gaseous and physical equilibria

slides.narration: Raising the pressure on a gas mixture favours the side with fewer moles of gas, and lowering it favours the side with more. If the number of moles of gas does not change there is no shift. Solids and liquids hardly respond. Ice melts under pressure because water takes up less volume than ice.

slides.heading: What a catalyst does
slides.body_md: A catalyst gives the reaction a path with a **lower activation energy** in **both directions equally**, so both rates rise by the same factor. It reaches equilibrium **sooner**, but the **composition**, **ΔH** and **K are unchanged**.

visual.caption: A catalyst lowers Ea in both directions.

slides.narration: This energy profile compares a reaction with and without a catalyst. The catalyst opens a path with a lower peak, so the activation energy falls for the forward and for the reverse reaction by the same amount. The starting and final energy levels are the same, so the enthalpy change and the equilibrium constant do not change.

slides.heading: Effect of an inert gas
slides.body_md: An inert gas takes no part in the reaction. **At constant volume** the concentrations of the reacting gases do not change: **no shift**. **At constant pressure** the volume increases, the concentrations fall, and the equilibrium shifts to the side with **more moles of gas**.

rows: For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI at constant pressure

visual.alt: Table comparing the effect of an inert gas at constant volume and at constant pressure

slides.narration: An inert gas takes no part in the reaction. If it is added at constant volume, the concentrations of the reacting gases do not change, so nothing shifts. If it is added at constant total pressure, the volume grows, the concentrations fall, and the equilibrium shifts to the side with more moles of gas.

slides.heading: Worked example: predicting shifts for methanol synthesis
slides.body_md: **Problem.** For $\ce{CO(g) + 2H2(g) <=> CH3OH(g)}$, $\Delta H = -90.7$ kJ, predict the effect on the yield of methanol of each change.

visual.alt: Table of predicted effects of five changes on the methanol synthesis equilibrium

slides.narration: The forward reaction releases heat, so raising the temperature pushes the equilibrium backward and lowers the yield. Raising the pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas, so the yield rises. Adding hydrogen or removing methanol shifts the equilibrium forward. A catalyst only helps the system reach equilibrium sooner.

slides.heading: Quick check: compression
slides.body_md: Count the moles of gas on each side before deciding.
slides.narration: Quick check. Compressing a gas mixture favours the side with fewer moles of gas. Count the moles of gas on each side of every equation, and pick the equilibrium in which the product side has fewer moles, so that compression increases the amount of product.

slides.heading: Worked example: pressure and the degree of dissociation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** At 330 K, $K_p = 0.50$ atm for $\ce{N2O4 <=> 2NO2}$, with $K_p = \dfrac{4\alpha^2P}{1-\alpha^2}$. Find α at $P = 1.0$ atm and at 4.0 atm.

$\alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_p}{K_p + 4P}}$: at 1.0 atm, $\alpha = \sqrt{0.50/4.50} = 0.333$; at 4.0 atm, $\alpha = \sqrt{0.50/16.5} = 0.174$.

visual.alt: Table of the degree of dissociation of dinitrogen tetroxide at three pressures

slides.narration: From the expression for Kp in terms of the degree of dissociation, solve for alpha. At one atmosphere it is one third. When the pressure is raised to four atmospheres the degree of dissociation falls to about seventeen percent, so high pressure keeps more nitrogen tetroxide, as Le Chatelier predicts.

slides.heading: Yield of ammonia against pressure and temperature
slides.body_md: In a model for **N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃** (ΔH = −92.4 kJ, ideal gases), the yield **rises with pressure** and **falls as temperature rises**. Industry uses about **200 atm** and a compromise temperature. Real gases give lower yields than this model.

visual.caption: Yield rises with pressure and falls as temperature rises (ideal-gas model).

slides.narration: This graph shows the model yield of ammonia against pressure for three temperatures. At every temperature the yield rises with pressure, because four moles of gas become two. At every pressure the yield is greater at the lower temperature, because the reaction gives out heat. This pushes us towards high pressure and low temperature.

slides.heading: Haber process: conditions
slides.body_md: **N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92.4 kJ.** Yield is favoured by **high pressure** (about **200 atm**) and **low temperature**, but a low temperature is too slow. **Compromise: about 700–720 K** with **finely divided iron** and a **molybdenum promoter**. **NH₃ is liquefied and removed**; N₂ and H₂ are **recycled**.

visual.alt: Table of the conditions chosen for the Haber process

slides.narration: In the Haber process the yield is favoured by high pressure and low temperature, but a low temperature makes the reaction too slow. So a compromise of about seven hundred kelvin is used, with finely divided iron as catalyst and molybdenum as promoter. High pressure is used too, and ammonia is removed as a liquid while the unused gases are recycled.

slides.heading: Contact process, N₂O₄ and ester equilibria

notes.title: Chemical Equilibrium — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Reversible and irreversible reactions; physical equilibria
sections.body_md:
An **irreversible** reaction goes (almost) to completion in one direction (magnesium burning in air). A **reversible** reaction can proceed in both directions (⇌); in a **closed vessel** it reaches **equilibrium**, with reactants and products present together.

**Physical equilibria** involve changes of state only, in a closed system at constant temperature: **solid ⇌ liquid** (ice ⇌ water at 273.15 K, 1 atm; constant melting point), **liquid ⇌ vapour** (water in a closed vessel; constant vapour pressure) and **solid ⇌ vapour** (iodine or camphor in a closed flask).

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction that can take place in both directions; in a closed vessel both reactants and products are present at equilibrium.
An equilibrium between two phases of the same substance, such as ice and water.

visual.alt: Table of the three types of physical equilibrium

sections.heading: 2. Dynamic nature and characteristics of equilibrium
sections.body_md:
At equilibrium the **rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction**; neither has stopped, so the equilibrium is **dynamic**. Evidence: heavy water added to liquid water in a closed vessel soon appears in the vapour although the vapour pressure is unchanged.

**Characteristics:** the system is closed at constant temperature; observable properties (concentration, pressure, colour) are constant; the same equilibrium is reached from either side (N₂O₄ or NO₂ as starting material); a **catalyst** speeds up the approach but does not change the position or K.

key_terms.definition_md: A state in which the forward and reverse changes continue at equal rates, so the macroscopic properties stay constant.

sections.heading: 3. Law of mass action; Kc and Kp
sections.body_md:
**Law of mass action:** at a given temperature the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient. For $a\text{A} + b\text{B} \rightleftharpoons c\text{C} + d\text{D}$ at equilibrium:

$K_c = \dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$ and, for gases, $K_p = \dfrac{p_C^c\,p_D^d}{p_A^a\,p_B^b}$.

Pure solids and liquids are left out (constant activity). **Units:** $K_c$ in (mol L⁻¹)^Δn and $K_p$ in (atm)^Δn, where Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants; no unit if Δn = 0.

key_terms.definition_md: The rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the molar concentrations of the reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient.
Moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants in the balanced equation.

visual.alt: Table of the units of Kc and Kp

sections.heading: 4. Relation between Kp and Kc (derivation); characteristics of K
sections.body_md:
**Derivation.** For an ideal gas $pV = nRT$, so $p = \dfrac{n}{V}RT = [\text{gas}]RT$. Substituting in $K_p$:

$K_p = \dfrac{([C]RT)^c([D]RT)^d}{([A]RT)^a([B]RT)^b} = \dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}(RT)^{(c+d)-(a+b)}$, so **$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$**. With R = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ for pressures in atm; $K_p = K_c$ when Δn = 0.

**Characteristics of K:** depends only on temperature; reverse the equation → 1/K; multiply the equation by n → Kⁿ; add equations → multiply the K values; independent of initial amounts, pressure and catalyst. Large K: products favoured; small K: reactants favoured. Recap from thermodynamics (Chapter 12): $\Delta G^\circ = -2.303\,RT\log K$, so a negative $\Delta G^\circ$ means $K > 1$.

key_terms.definition_md: The same expression as K evaluated with non-equilibrium concentrations; Q < K means the net reaction goes forward, Q > K backward.

visual.alt: Table of the effect of changing the equation on K

sections.heading: 5. Equilibrium calculations
sections.body_md:
**ICE method:** write Initial, Change (use x or α) and Equilibrium amounts; substitute in K. **Esterification** ($K_c = 4.0$): 1.0 mol acid + 1.0 mol alcohol gives x²/(1 − x)² = 4, x = 0.67 mol of ester; with 1.0 mol acid and 3.0 mol alcohol, 3x² − 16x + 12 = 0 and x = 0.903 mol (the excess alcohol raises the conversion).

**Degree of dissociation α** of N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ at total pressure P: moles 1 − α, 2α, total 1 + α, so $K_p = \dfrac{4\alpha^2P}{1-\alpha^2}$ and $\alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_p}{K_p + 4P}}$. With K_p = 0.50 atm at 330 K and P = 1.0 atm, α = 0.333. Also α = M(theoretical) / M(observed) − 1.

**Br₂ + Cl₂ ⇌ 2BrCl** ($K_c = 7.0$): when the starting amounts are equal take the square root of K_c: 2x/(c − x) = 2.646.

key_terms.definition_md: The fraction of the original amount of a substance that has dissociated at equilibrium.
Initial, change and equilibrium rows used to find equilibrium amounts.

sections.heading: 6. Le Chatelier's principle and conditions for maximum yield
sections.body_md:
**Le Chatelier's principle:** if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change of concentration, temperature or pressure, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that opposes the change.

**Concentration:** adding a reactant or removing a product shifts forward (K unchanged). **Temperature:** raising T favours the endothermic direction and changes K (increases for endothermic, decreases for exothermic). **Pressure:** raising P favours the side with fewer moles of gas; no effect if Δn = 0. **Catalyst:** lowers the activation energy of both directions equally; no change of position or K. **Inert gas:** at constant volume no shift; at constant pressure the volume increases and the equilibrium shifts to the side with more moles of gas.

**Haber process** (ΔH = −92.4 kJ): about 200 atm, 700–720 K, Fe with Mo promoter; NH₃ liquefied and removed, gases recycled. **Contact process** (ΔH = −196 kJ): about 720–725 K, 1–2 atm, V₂O₅. **N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂** (endothermic, 1 → 2 mol): high T, low P. **Ester hydrolysis** (Δn = 0): excess water, remove a product, pressure has no effect; **esterification**: excess alcohol, conc. H₂SO₄ removes water.

key_terms.definition_md: A system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by shifting in the direction that opposes the disturbance.
A substance that improves the action of a catalyst, such as molybdenum with iron in the Haber process.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Including pure solids or liquids in K, or using moles instead of concentrations.
- Forgetting that Δn counts gaseous species only, or using °C in RT.
- Saying a catalyst increases the yield, or that pressure changes K.
- Applying a pressure argument when Δn = 0, or to a reaction in solution.
- Not saying whether the volume or the pressure is constant when an inert gas is added.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Derivation of Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn: p = [gas]RT (1), substitution (1), Δn defined and result (1).
- Equilibrium numericals: expression (1), ICE amounts (1), solving (1), unit (1).
- Le Chatelier predictions: direction (1) and the reason, using ΔH or Δn (1).
- Industrial conditions: pressure with reason (1), temperature as a compromise (1), catalyst (1).

cards.front_md: What is a reversible reaction?
cards.back_md: One that can proceed in both directions; in a closed vessel reactants and products coexist at equilibrium.

cards.front_md: Name the three physical equilibria.
cards.back_md: Solid ⇌ liquid, liquid ⇌ vapour, solid ⇌ vapour.

cards.front_md: Condition for the ice–water equilibrium?
cards.back_md: 273.15 K and 1 atm.

cards.front_md: Property that is constant in a liquid–vapour equilibrium?
cards.back_md: The vapour pressure at that temperature.

cards.front_md: Why is chemical equilibrium called dynamic?
cards.back_md: Forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; nothing has stopped.

cards.front_md: Which evidence shows that equilibrium is dynamic?
cards.back_md: Heavy water added to liquid water in a closed vessel appears in the vapour although the pressure stays constant.

cards.front_md: Can equilibrium be reached from either side?
cards.back_md: Yes: the same composition results at a given temperature.

cards.front_md: State the law of mass action.
cards.back_md: The rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the molar concentrations (active masses) of the reactants, each raised to its coefficient.

cards.front_md: Write Kc for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD.
cards.back_md: $K_c = \dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$

cards.front_md: Which species are left out of K?
cards.back_md: Pure solids and pure liquids.

cards.front_md: Write Kp for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
cards.back_md: $K_p = \dfrac{p_{NH_3}^2}{p_{N_2}\,p_{H_2}^3}$, unit atm⁻².

cards.front_md: Define Δn for Kp and Kc.
cards.back_md: Moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants.

cards.front_md: Unit of Kc when Δn = +1?
cards.back_md: mol L⁻¹.

cards.front_md: Unit of Kc for 2NO + O₂ ⇌ 2NO₂?
cards.back_md: L mol⁻¹ (Δn = −1).

cards.front_md: Relation between Kp and Kc?
cards.back_md: $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$

cards.front_md: First step in deriving Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn?
cards.back_md: Use pV = nRT to write p = (n/V)RT = [gas]RT for each gas.

cards.front_md: When is Kp = Kc?
cards.back_md: When Δn = 0, for example H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI.

cards.front_md: What happens to K when an equation is reversed?
What happens to K when two equations are added?
cards.back_md: The K values are multiplied.

cards.front_md: What does K depend on?
cards.back_md: Temperature only.

cards.front_md: Kp of N₂O₄ in terms of α and total pressure P?
cards.back_md: $K_p = \dfrac{4\alpha^2 P}{1-\alpha^2}$

cards.front_md: State Le Chatelier's principle.
cards.back_md: A system at equilibrium responds to a change of concentration, temperature or pressure by shifting in the direction that opposes the change.

cards.front_md: Effect of raising the temperature on an exothermic equilibrium?
cards.back_md: Shifts backward; K decreases.

cards.front_md: Effect of raising the pressure?
cards.back_md: Favours the side with fewer moles of gas; none if Δn = 0.

cards.front_md: Effect of a catalyst on equilibrium?
cards.back_md: Faster approach only: no change in position, composition or K.

cards.front_md: Inert gas added at constant volume?
cards.back_md: No shift: the concentrations are unchanged.

cards.front_md: Inert gas added at constant pressure?
cards.back_md: The volume increases; the equilibrium shifts to the side with more moles of gas.

cards.front_md: Conditions for the Haber process?
cards.back_md: About 200 atm, 700–720 K, finely divided iron with molybdenum promoter; NH₃ removed and gases recycled.

cards.front_md: Conditions for the contact process?
cards.back_md: About 720–725 K, 1–2 atm, V₂O₅ catalyst.

cards.front_md: Conditions that give maximum NO₂ from N₂O₄?
cards.back_md: High temperature (endothermic) and low pressure (1 → 2 mol).

cards.front_md: How is the yield of an ester increased?
cards.back_md: Excess alcohol or acid and removal of water (conc. H₂SO₄) or of the ester.

cards.front_md: Why has pressure no effect on ester hydrolysis?
cards.back_md: Δn_g = 0 and the reaction takes place in the liquid phase.

questions.stem_md: A chemistry teacher shows four changes. Which one is, for practical purposes, irreversible under ordinary laboratory conditions?

options.text_md: liquid bromine and its vapour in a stoppered bottle
a strip of magnesium burning in air in an open dish
solid iodine and its vapour in a sealed flask
brown NO₂ gas and colourless N₂O₄ gas in a closed tube

questions.solution_md: Burning magnesium forms magnesium oxide, which does not turn back to the metal and oxygen under these conditions, and the products escape the system. The other three are changes in closed vessels in which both directions go on — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Crushed ice and water are kept in a closed insulated flask at 273.15 K and 1 atm until the amount of ice stops changing. At this stage:

options.text_md: ice melts and water freezes at the same rate
melting has stopped but freezing continues
freezing has stopped but melting continues
neither melting nor freezing is taking place

questions.solution_md: A solid–liquid equilibrium is dynamic: the amount of ice stays constant because the rate of melting equals the rate of freezing, not because both processes have stopped — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a sealed bottle kept at constant temperature, a sample of ethanol and its vapour are left for several hours. The vapour pressure becomes constant because:

options.text_md: all the liquid has changed to vapour
no more molecules can escape from the liquid
the molecules of vapour have stopped moving
the number of molecules leaving the liquid per second equals the number returning to it

questions.solution_md: When the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation the vapour pressure stays constant; the equilibrium is dynamic and both processes continue — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A few crystals of iodine are sealed in a glass flask at 30 °C. After some days a constant violet colour fills the flask and crystals are still present. The system shows:

options.text_md: a liquid–vapour equilibrium, with evaporation and condensation at equal rates
a solid–liquid equilibrium, with melting and freezing at equal rates
a solid–vapour equilibrium, with sublimation and deposition at equal rates
an irreversible change, since the crystals are slowly disappearing

questions.solution_md: Solid iodine changes directly to vapour (sublimation) and the vapour deposits as crystals. The constant colour and the persisting crystals show that both rates are equal, a solid–vapour equilibrium — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A few drops of heavy water (D₂O) added to liquid water in a closed vessel at equilibrium are soon found in the vapour, although the vapour pressure does not change.

**Reason (R):** At equilibrium evaporation and condensation continue at equal rates.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Molecules keep passing from liquid to vapour and back, so the label appears in the vapour; the pressure stays constant because the two rates are equal. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A chemical equilibrium can be established only in a closed system, and it can be approached from either the reactant side or the product side.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. In an open vessel products can escape and equilibrium is not reached; in a closed vessel the same equilibrium composition is reached from either side at a given temperature.

questions.stem_md: Name the three types of physical equilibrium and give one example of each, with the condition under which it holds.

answer.model_answer_md: Solid–liquid: ice ⇌ water at 273.15 K and 1 atm. Liquid–vapour: water ⇌ water vapour in a closed vessel at constant temperature. Solid–vapour: iodine (or camphor) crystals ⇌ vapour in a closed flask at constant temperature.

questions.solution_md: Solid–liquid, liquid–vapour, solid–vapour with one example each.

marking_scheme.step: An example with the condition for each

questions.stem_md: List four characteristics of a system that has reached chemical equilibrium.

answer.model_answer_md: The system must be closed, at constant temperature. The macroscopic properties (concentration, pressure, colour) stay constant. The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, so the equilibrium is dynamic. The same state is reached from either side, and a catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.

questions.solution_md: Closed system; constant properties; equal rates (dynamic); same state from either side; catalyst has no effect on position.

questions.stem_md:
A student seals 20 mL of water at 25 °C in a flask and measures the pressure of the vapour above it every ten minutes. The pressure rises at first and then becomes constant.

(a) Explain the rise and then the constant value, in terms of the rates of the two opposing changes. [2]

(b) Name this type of equilibrium and name one more physical equilibrium of the solid–vapour type. [1]

(c) Why is the equilibrium called dynamic? Describe an observation that supports your answer. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) At first the rate of evaporation is high and the rate of condensation is almost zero, so the vapour pressure rises. As vapour builds up the rate of condensation rises while evaporation continues at the same rate. When the two rates become equal, the number of molecules in the vapour no longer changes and the pressure is constant.

(b) Liquid–vapour equilibrium. Solid–vapour: iodine or camphor in a closed flask.

(c) Both changes go on at equal rates; nothing has stopped. If a trace of heavy water (or a radioactive tracer) is added to the liquid, it appears in the vapour after a while, although the amount of liquid and the pressure stay constant.

questions.solution_md: Rates equal at the constant pressure; liquid–vapour; dynamic shown by tracer in the vapour.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Rising evaporation rate against low condensation rate at first
(b) Liquid–vapour equilibrium and one solid–vapour example
(c) Both processes continue at equal rates

questions.stem_md: In an industrial reactor all the species of $\ce{4NH3(g) + 5O2(g) <=> 4NO(g) + 6H2O(g)}$ are gases. The expression for $K_c$ is:

options.text_md: $\dfrac{[\text{NH}_3]^4[\text{O}_2]^5}{[\text{NO}]^4[\text{H}_2\text{O}]^6}$
$\dfrac{[\text{NO}]^4[\text{H}_2\text{O}]^6}{[\text{NH}_3]^4[\text{O}_2]^5}$
$\dfrac{4[\text{NO}]\times 6[\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{4[\text{NH}_3]\times 5[\text{O}_2]}$
$\dfrac{[\text{NO}]^6[\text{H}_2\text{O}]^4}{[\text{NH}_3]^5[\text{O}_2]^4}$

questions.solution_md: By the law of mass action K_c is the product of the equilibrium concentrations of the products, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, divided by the same for the reactants: [NO]⁴[H₂O]⁶ / ([NH₃]⁴[O₂]⁵) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{2NO(g) + Cl2(g) <=> 2NOCl(g)}$ the equilibrium constant $K_p$ is calculated from partial pressures in atm. Its unit is:

options.text_md: $\text{atm}$
$\text{atm}^{-1}$
$\text{atm}^{-2}$
no unit

questions.solution_md: Δn_g = 2 − 3 = −1, so K_p = p²(NOCl) / (p²(NO) × p(Cl₂)) has the unit atm² / atm³ = atm⁻¹ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: For which of the following gaseous reactions is the numerical value of Kp equal to that of Kc at the same temperature?
questions.solution_md: K_p = K_c (RT)^Δn, so K_p = K_c only when Δn_g = 0. N₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO has 2 mol of gas on each side (Δn = 0); the others have Δn = +2, +1 and −1 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Carbon is heated in a closed furnace with carbon dioxide: $\ce{C(s) + CO2(g) <=> 2CO(g)}$. The expression for $K_p$ is:

options.text_md: $K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{CO}}^2}{p_{\text{C}}\,p_{\text{CO}_2}}$
$K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{CO}_2}}{p_{\text{CO}}^2}$
$K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{CO}}}{p_{\text{CO}_2}}$
$K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{CO}}^2}{p_{\text{CO}_2}}$

questions.solution_md: The activity of a pure solid is constant and is not written in the expression. Only the gases appear: K_p = p²(CO) / p(CO₂) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: At a certain temperature $K_c = 25$ (given) for $\ce{2NO2(g) <=> N2O4(g)}$. The equilibrium constant for $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$ at the same temperature is:
questions.solution_md: Reversing an equation inverts K: K′ = 1 / 25 = 0.04 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: At a given temperature (data given) $\ce{N2 + O2 <=> 2NO}$ has $K_c = 1.0 \times 10^{-30}$ and $\ce{2NO + O2 <=> 2NO2}$ has $K_c = 3.0 \times 10^{12}$. The $K_c$ of $\ce{N2 + 2O2 <=> 2NO2}$ at that temperature is:
questions.solution_md: Adding two equations multiplies their K values: K = K₁ × K₂ = (1.0 × 10⁻³⁰)(3.0 × 10¹²) = 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁸ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a closed 1.0 L vessel at 1000 K, $K_c = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L⁻¹ (given) for $\ce{2H2S(g) <=> 2H2(g) + S2(g)}$. A mixture is prepared with $[\text{H}_2\text{S}] = 0.20$, $[\text{H}_2] = 0.040$ and $[\text{S}_2] = 0.030$ mol L⁻¹. The mixture will:

options.text_md: move towards H₂ and S₂, because the reaction quotient is greater than K_c
stay as it is, because the reaction quotient equals K_c
move towards H₂S, because the reaction quotient (1.2 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹) is greater than K_c
move towards H₂ and S₂, because the reaction quotient is less than K_c

questions.solution_md: Q = [H₂]²[S₂] / [H₂S]² = (0.040)²(0.030) / (0.20)² = 1.2 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹. Since Q > K_c (1.0 × 10⁻³), the net reaction goes backward until Q = K_c — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The molar mass of pure $\ce{N2O4}$ is 92 g mol⁻¹. A sample of $\ce{N2O4(g)}$ in a closed vessel dissociates into $\ce{NO2(g)}$ at 330 K and the average molar mass of the equilibrium mixture is found to be 69 g mol⁻¹. The degree of dissociation of $\ce{N2O4}$ is:
questions.solution_md: One mole of N₂O₄ gives 1 + α moles of gas, and the mass is unchanged, so M(observed) = 92 / (1 + α). 69 = 92 / (1 + α) gives 1 + α = 1.333, so α = 0.33 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{CH3COOH(l) + C2H5OH(l) <=> CH3COOC2H5(l) + H2O(l)}$, $K_c = 4.0$ at room temperature. One mole of ethanoic acid is mixed with one mole of ethanol and left to reach equilibrium. The amount of ethyl ethanoate formed is:

options.text_md: 1.00 mol
0.50 mol
0.67 mol
0.80 mol

questions.solution_md: Let x mol of ester form. K_c = x² / (1 − x)² = 4.0 (volume cancels because Δn = 0), so x / (1 − x) = 2 and x = 0.67 mol — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The equilibrium constant $K_c$ of $\ce{2HI(g) <=> H2(g) + I2(g)}$ has no unit.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The number of moles of gas is the same on both sides (Δn = 0), so the concentration units cancel in K_c = [H₂][I₂] / [HI]².

questions.stem_md: In the expression for Kp the concentrations of the gases are replaced by their ___ at equilibrium.
questions.solution_md: K_p is written with the partial pressures of the gases.

questions.stem_md: The unit of $K_c$ for $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}$ is ___ (write it as L to a power and mol to a power).
questions.solution_md: Δn_g = −2, so the unit is (mol L⁻¹)⁻² = L² mol⁻².

questions.stem_md: Match each gaseous reaction in Column I with the unit of its Kc in Column II (concentrations in mol L⁻¹).
questions.solution_md: The unit is (mol L⁻¹)^Δn: Δn = 0 gives no unit, Δn = +1 gives mol L⁻¹, Δn = −1 gives L mol⁻¹ and Δn = −2 gives L² mol⁻².

questions.stem_md: State the law of mass action and use it to write the equilibrium constant expression $K_c$ for the general gaseous reaction $\ce{aA + bB <=> cC + dD}$.

answer.model_answer_md: At a given temperature the rate of a chemical reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, which gives $K_c = \dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$, a constant at a given temperature.

questions.solution_md: Rate ∝ product of active masses; K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b).

marking_scheme.step: Statement of the law of mass action

questions.stem_md: Write $K_c$ and $K_p$ for $\ce{NH4Cl(s) <=> NH3(g) + HCl(g)}$ and explain why the solid is left out of the expressions.

answer.model_answer_md: K_c = [NH₃][HCl] and K_p = p(NH₃) × p(HCl). The concentration of a pure solid is constant at a given temperature (its density divided by its molar mass), so it is taken into the constant and does not appear in the expression.

questions.solution_md: K_c = [NH₃][HCl]; K_p = p(NH₃)p(HCl); the activity of a pure solid is constant.

marking_scheme.step: K_c and K_p expressions without the solid
Reason: constant concentration of a pure solid

questions.stem_md: A student states three facts about an equilibrium constant. Say which factors change K and which do not: (i) the starting concentrations, (ii) the temperature, (iii) the presence of a catalyst, (iv) the total pressure.

answer.model_answer_md: Only the temperature (ii) changes the equilibrium constant. The starting concentrations (i), the catalyst (iii) and the pressure (iv) do not change K, although they may change how much of each substance is present or how fast equilibrium is reached.

questions.solution_md: Only temperature changes K.

marking_scheme.step: Concentration, catalyst and pressure do not

questions.stem_md: In a closed furnace at 600 K the equilibrium $\ce{COCl2(g) <=> CO(g) + Cl2(g)}$ has partial pressures 0.80 atm of $\ce{COCl2}$, 0.20 atm of $\ce{CO}$ and 0.20 atm of $\ce{Cl2}$ (given). Calculate $K_p$ in atm.
questions.solution_md: $K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{CO}}\,p_{\text{Cl}_2}}{p_{\text{COCl}_2}} = \dfrac{0.20 \times 0.20}{0.80} = 0.05$ atm.

questions.stem_md: A 2.0 L closed vessel at 1000 K holds, at equilibrium, 0.50 mol $\ce{H2S}$, 0.10 mol $\ce{H2}$ and 0.050 mol $\ce{S2}$ (given), all gases, in the reaction $\ce{2H2S(g) <=> 2H2(g) + S2(g)}$. Calculate $K_c$ in mol L⁻¹.
For the methanol synthesis $\ce{CO(g) + 2H2(g) <=> CH3OH(g)}$ at 500 K, $K_c = 14.5$ L² mol⁻² (given). Calculate $K_p$ in atm⁻² ($R = 0.0821$ L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).

marking_scheme.step: RT = 41.05 L atm mol⁻¹ and K_p = 8.6 × 10⁻³ atm⁻²

questions.stem_md: Solid ammonium hydrogensulphide is placed in an evacuated flask at 298 K and decomposes: $\ce{NH4HS(s) <=> NH3(g) + H2S(g)}$. At equilibrium the total pressure is 0.66 atm (given). Calculate $K_p$ and $K_c$ ($R = 0.0821$ L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).

answer.model_answer_md: Only the gases appear, and they are formed in equal amounts, so p(NH₃) = p(H₂S) = 0.66 / 2 = 0.33 atm. K_p = p(NH₃) × p(H₂S) = 0.33 × 0.33 = 0.1089 atm². Δn_g = 2, so K_c = K_p / (RT)² = 0.1089 / (0.0821 × 298)² = 0.1089 / 598.6 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ mol² L⁻².

questions.solution_md: K_p = 0.1089 atm²; K_c = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ mol² L⁻².

questions.stem_md: Bromine monochloride forms in a sealed 1.0 L vessel at 400 K: $\ce{Br2(g) + Cl2(g) <=> 2BrCl(g)}$, $K_c = 7.0$. The vessel is filled with 0.20 mol of $\ce{Br2}$ and 0.20 mol of $\ce{Cl2}$ only. Calculate the equilibrium concentration of $\ce{BrCl}$.

answer.model_answer_md: Let x mol L⁻¹ of Br₂ react. [Br₂] = [Cl₂] = 0.20 − x and [BrCl] = 2x. K_c = (2x)² / (0.20 − x)² = 7.0, so 2x / (0.20 − x) = √7.0 = 2.646. Then 2x = 0.5292 − 2.646x, giving x = 0.1139 mol L⁻¹. [BrCl] = 2x = 0.228 mol L⁻¹ (and [Br₂] = [Cl₂] = 0.086 mol L⁻¹).

questions.solution_md: [BrCl] = 0.228 mol L⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: Square root of K_c taken: 2x / (0.20 − x) = 2.646

questions.stem_md: A different experiment at 400 K starts with 0.60 mol L⁻¹ of $\ce{BrCl}$ alone in a closed vessel, which decomposes to $\ce{Br2}$ and $\ce{Cl2}$ ($K_c = 7.0$ for the formation of BrCl from the elements). Calculate the equilibrium concentrations of all three species.

answer.model_answer_md: 2BrCl ⇌ Br₂ + Cl₂ has K_c′ = 1 / 7.0 = 0.1429. Let x mol L⁻¹ of Br₂ form: [Br₂] = [Cl₂] = x and [BrCl] = 0.60 − 2x. x² / (0.60 − 2x)² = 1 / 7.0, so x / (0.60 − 2x) = 0.378 and x = 0.1292 mol L⁻¹. [Br₂] = [Cl₂] = 0.129 and [BrCl] = 0.342 mol L⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: [Br₂] = [Cl₂] = 0.129; [BrCl] = 0.342 mol L⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: Equilibrium concentrations x, x and 0.60 − 2x; square root taken

questions.stem_md: A flask holds 1.0 mol of ethanoic acid and 3.0 mol of ethanol at room temperature, with the equilibrium $\ce{CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O}$, $K_c = 4.0$. Calculate the amount of ester at equilibrium and compare the conversion of the acid with that when 1.0 mol each of acid and alcohol are used (0.67 mol of ester).

answer.model_answer_md: Let x mol of ester form: x² / ((1 − x)(3 − x)) = 4.0, so 3x² − 16x + 12 = 0 and x = 0.903 mol (the other root, 4.43, exceeds the acid present). The conversion of the acid is 90%, against 67% with equal amounts. The excess of alcohol drives the equilibrium forward (Le Chatelier).

questions.solution_md: x = 0.903 mol; 90% against 67%.

marking_scheme.step: Equation x² = 4(1 − x)(3 − x) rearranged to 3x² − 16x + 12 = 0
x = 0.903 mol, root less than 1 chosen
Higher conversion with excess alcohol, explained

questions.stem_md:
(a) For the gaseous equilibrium $\ce{aA + bB <=> cC + dD}$, derive the relation $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$, defining $\Delta n$. [3]

(b) For $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$, $K_c = 4.6 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L⁻¹ at 298 K (given). Calculate $K_p$ in atm ($R = 0.0821$ L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For an ideal gas $pV = nRT$, so the partial pressure of a gas is $p = \dfrac{n}{V}RT = [\,\text{gas}\,]RT$. Then
$K_p = \dfrac{p_C^c\,p_D^d}{p_A^a\,p_B^b} = \dfrac{([C]RT)^c([D]RT)^d}{([A]RT)^a([B]RT)^b} = \dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}\,(RT)^{(c+d)-(a+b)}$.
So $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$, where $\Delta n = (c + d) - (a + b)$ is the change in the number of moles of gas on going from reactants to products.

(b) $\Delta n = 2 - 1 = +1$, so $K_p = K_c(RT) = 4.6 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.0821 \times 298 = 0.113$ atm.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Partial pressure p = [gas]RT from pV = nRT
(a) Substitution in K_p and grouping the RT terms
(a) Δn = (c + d) − (a + b), result K_p = K_c (RT)^Δn

questions.stem_md:
(a) One mole of $\ce{N2O4}$ dissociates to the extent α at total pressure P: $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$. Derive $K_p$ in terms of α and P. [3]

(b) At 330 K, $K_p = 0.50$ atm (given). Calculate the degree of dissociation at a total pressure of 2.0 atm. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Moles at equilibrium: $\ce{N2O4}$: $1 - \alpha$; $\ce{NO2}$: $2\alpha$; total $1 + \alpha$. Mole fractions $\dfrac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}$ and $\dfrac{2\alpha}{1+\alpha}$; partial pressures are these times $P$.
$K_p = \dfrac{p_{NO_2}^2}{p_{N_2O_4}} = \dfrac{4\alpha^2P^2/(1+\alpha)^2}{(1-\alpha)P/(1+\alpha)} = \dfrac{4\alpha^2P}{1-\alpha^2}$.

(b) $0.50 = \dfrac{4\alpha^2(2.0)}{1-\alpha^2}$, so $0.50(1-\alpha^2) = 8.0\alpha^2$, $\alpha^2 = \dfrac{0.50}{8.5} = 0.0588$ and $\alpha = 0.24$ (about 24%).

marking_scheme.step: (a) Partial pressures from mole fractions × P

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At a fixed temperature the equilibrium constant of a reaction does not change when more of a reactant is added to the equilibrium mixture.

**Reason (R):** The equilibrium constant depends on the initial concentrations of the reactants.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: adding a reactant disturbs the equilibrium, which shifts to restore the same K at that temperature. R is false: K does not depend on the initial concentrations; it depends only on temperature — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For $\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$ the numerical values of $K_p$ and $K_c$ are equal.

**Reason (R):** The total number of moles of gas changes during this reaction.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: Δn_g = 2 − 2 = 0, so K_p = K_c (RT)⁰ = K_c. R is false: the number of moles of gas does not change, which is exactly why they are equal — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A few drops of iron(III) nitrate and potassium thiocyanate give a red solution in the equilibrium $\ce{Fe^3+(aq) + SCN-(aq) <=> FeSCN^2+(aq)}$. More iron(III) nitrate solution is now added. The red colour:

options.text_md: fades, as the equilibrium shifts to the left
becomes deeper, as the equilibrium shifts to the right
is unchanged, as K does not change
turns yellow, as thiocyanate is removed completely

questions.solution_md: Adding Fe³⁺ raises a reactant concentration, so the system shifts to the right to use up some of it, forming more of the red complex. K is unchanged but the position of equilibrium moves — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Orange potassium dichromate solution contains the equilibrium $\ce{Cr2O7^2-(aq) + H2O(l) <=> 2CrO4^2-(aq) + 2H+(aq)}$ (yellow chromate on the right). A student adds dilute sodium hydroxide dropwise. The colour changes to:

options.text_md: deeper orange, because OH⁻ removes H⁺ and the equilibrium shifts to the left
yellow, because OH⁻ adds to the chromate and the equilibrium shifts to the left
no change, because water is a pure liquid in the expression
yellow, because OH⁻ removes H⁺ and the equilibrium shifts to the right

questions.solution_md: OH⁻ ions neutralise H⁺ ions, lowering [H⁺]. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts to the right to replace H⁺, forming more yellow CrO₄²⁻ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A sealed tube of brown $\ce{NO2}$ and colourless $\ce{N2O4}$ at equilibrium, $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$ with $\Delta H = +57.2$ kJ, is placed in hot water. The tube:

options.text_md: darkens, because the endothermic forward reaction is favoured by a rise in temperature
becomes paler, because the exothermic reaction is favoured by a rise in temperature
darkens, because the value of K decreases
is unchanged, because the total pressure is constant

questions.solution_md: Heating shifts the equilibrium in the direction that absorbs heat, the forward (endothermic) reaction. More brown NO₂ forms and the equilibrium constant increases — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In which of the following gaseous equilibria will compressing the mixture at constant temperature increase the amount of product?

options.text_md: $\ce{CO(g) + 2H2(g) <=> CH3OH(g)}$

questions.solution_md: Compression favours the side with fewer moles of gas. CO + 2H₂ ⇌ CH₃OH goes from 3 mol to 1 mol, so the product increases. N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ and 2NH₃ ⇌ N₂ + 3H₂ would shift backward, and H₂ + Cl₂ ⇌ 2HCl is unaffected — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A sealed container holds an equilibrium mixture of H₂, I₂ and HI gases. Halving the volume of the container at constant temperature will:

options.text_md: shift the equilibrium towards HI
shift the equilibrium towards H₂ and I₂
change the value of the equilibrium constant
double all the concentrations without shifting the position of equilibrium

questions.solution_md: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI has 2 mol of gas on each side, so pressure does not favour either direction. Halving the volume doubles all the concentrations, and Q stays equal to K — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Carbon dioxide passes over red-hot coke in a furnace: $\ce{C(s) + CO2(g) <=> 2CO(g)}$, $\Delta H = +172$ kJ. Which change increases the percentage of $\ce{CO}$ in the gas at equilibrium?

options.text_md: raising the temperature and raising the total pressure
raising the temperature and lowering the total pressure
lowering the temperature and lowering the total pressure
adding more solid carbon at constant temperature and volume

questions.solution_md: The reaction is endothermic, so a higher temperature favours CO. It increases the moles of gas (1 → 2), so a lower pressure also favours CO. Adding more solid carbon changes nothing, since a pure solid does not appear in K — option (b).

questions.stem_md: At 330 K and constant total pressure, $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$ is at equilibrium. Argon is now added so that the pressure stays constant (the volume increases). The amount of $\ce{NO2}$:

options.text_md: increases, because the partial pressures fall and the side with more moles of gas is favoured
decreases, because the total number of moles of gas increases
stays the same, because argon takes no part in the reaction
decreases, because the volume of the container increases

questions.solution_md: At constant total pressure, adding argon increases the volume, so the partial pressures and concentrations of N₂O₄ and NO₂ all fall. The system behaves as if the pressure were lowered and shifts to the side with more gas moles, producing more NO₂ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Argon is added to the equilibrium mixture in $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}$ at constant volume. The equilibrium shifts towards the side with more moles of gas.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. At constant volume the concentrations of the reacting gases do not change when an inert gas is added, so Q stays equal to K and the equilibrium does not shift.

questions.stem_md: Two reactors hold the same gaseous reversible reaction starting from identical mixtures; a catalyst is used in one only. Compared with the uncatalysed reactor, the catalysed reactor:

options.text_md: reaches equilibrium sooner and with more product
reaches equilibrium at the same time but with more product
reaches equilibrium sooner but with a larger value of K
reaches equilibrium sooner but with the same composition and the same value of K

questions.solution_md: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and the reverse reactions by the same amount, so both rates rise equally. Equilibrium is reached faster, but K and the equilibrium composition are unchanged — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A sealed bottle of soda contains $\ce{CO2(g) <=> CO2(aq)}$ under pressure. When the cap is opened, gas bubbles out of the drink because:

options.text_md: the pressure falls and more CO₂ dissolves to replace the lost gas
the temperature falls and CO₂ becomes more soluble
the equilibrium constant of dissolution falls to zero
the pressure falls and the equilibrium shifts to the side with the gas, so dissolved CO₂ comes out

questions.solution_md: Opening the cap lowers the pressure of CO₂ above the liquid. The equilibrium shifts in the direction that raises the gas pressure, so CO₂(aq) changes to CO₂(g) and bubbles form — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The equilibrium constant of an exothermic reaction decreases when the temperature is raised.

**Reason (R):** Ice floats on liquid water because ice is less dense than water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction, so K falls for an exothermic reaction. The density of ice is a true fact about water that has nothing to do with the temperature effect on K, so R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Increasing the pressure on $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$ at constant temperature favours the forward reaction.

**Reason (R):** The forward reaction decreases the number of moles of gas.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are false. The forward reaction increases the moles of gas (1 → 2), so a higher pressure favours the reverse reaction, towards N₂O₄ — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Raising the pressure on ice and water at 273 K melts some of the ice.

**Reason (R):** The volume of a given mass of water is less than that of the same mass of ice, so melting reduces the volume.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Ice is less dense than water, so melting decreases the volume. By Le Chatelier's principle higher pressure favours the change that reduces the volume — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A reversible gas-phase reaction in a plant is already at equilibrium when a catalyst is added to the reactor. State and justify what happens to (i) the composition of the mixture and (ii) the value of the equilibrium constant.

answer.model_answer_md: Both unchanged. A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and the reverse reactions equally, so it speeds up both rates by the same factor. The rates remain equal, so the composition does not alter, and K, which depends only on temperature, is unchanged. Had equilibrium not been reached, the catalyst would help to reach it sooner.

questions.solution_md: No change in composition or K; both rates increase equally.

questions.stem_md: Explain how adding helium to the equilibrium mixture of $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$ affects the position of equilibrium (i) at constant volume and (ii) at constant total pressure.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) At constant volume the concentrations (partial pressures) of N₂O₄ and NO₂ are unchanged, so there is no shift. (ii) At constant pressure the volume increases, so the concentrations fall, as if the pressure were lowered; the equilibrium shifts to the side with more moles of gas, towards NO₂.

questions.solution_md: No shift at constant V; shift towards NO₂ at constant P.

marking_scheme.step: (i) No change at constant volume, with reason
(ii) Shift towards NO₂ at constant pressure, with reason

questions.stem_md: Methanol is made in a closed reactor by $\ce{CO(g) + 2H2(g) <=> CH3OH(g)}$, $\Delta H = -90.7$ kJ. Predict, with reasons, the effect on the yield of methanol of (i) raising the temperature, (ii) raising the pressure and (iii) removing methanol as it forms.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The forward reaction is exothermic, so a rise in temperature favours the reverse reaction; K falls and the yield decreases. (ii) The forward reaction reduces the moles of gas (3 → 1), so a higher pressure shifts the equilibrium forward and the yield increases. (iii) Removing the product lowers its concentration below the equilibrium value, so the system shifts forward and more methanol forms.

questions.solution_md: Yield: lower with higher T; higher with higher P; higher when methanol is removed.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Higher yield, product removal shifts forward

questions.stem_md: Producer gas contains the equilibrium $\ce{C(s) + CO2(g) <=> 2CO(g)}$, $\Delta H = +172$ kJ. State, with reasons, how the amount of $\ce{CO}$ at equilibrium changes when (i) the temperature is raised, (ii) the volume is halved at constant temperature, and (iii) more solid carbon is added.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The forward reaction is endothermic, so higher temperature favours CO: its amount increases. (ii) Halving the volume doubles the pressure; the forward reaction increases the moles of gas (1 → 2), so the equilibrium shifts back and the amount of CO decreases. (iii) No change: pure solid carbon has constant activity and does not appear in K_c, so the position does not alter.

questions.solution_md: CO increases with T; decreases on compression; no change with more carbon.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Decrease, fewer gas moles on the left
(iii) No change, solid not in K

questions.stem_md: Dilute acid is added dropwise to a yellow solution of chromate ions until the colour turns orange: $\ce{2CrO4^2-(aq) + 2H+(aq) <=> Cr2O7^2-(aq) + H2O(l)}$. Explain the colour change, and say what is seen when sodium hydroxide solution is then added in excess.

answer.model_answer_md: Adding H⁺ raises the concentration of a reactant, so the equilibrium shifts to the right; the yellow CrO₄²⁻ is used up and orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ forms. Adding excess NaOH removes H⁺ (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O), so the equilibrium shifts to the left and the yellow colour returns. K does not change in either case.

questions.solution_md: Acid: shift right, orange; alkali: shift left, yellow.

marking_scheme.step: Acid shifts the equilibrium right: orange
Alkali removes H⁺ and shifts it left: yellow

questions.stem_md: The equilibrium constant Kc of a gaseous reaction A ⇌ B was measured (data given): 120 at 300 K, 15 at 400 K and 3.0 at 500 K. Decide whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and predict what happens to the percentage of B at equilibrium as the temperature is raised.

answer.model_answer_md: K decreases as the temperature rises, so the equilibrium is shifted towards the reactant A. By Le Chatelier's principle, a rise in temperature favours the endothermic direction; here that is the reverse direction, so the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH < 0). The percentage of B in the equilibrium mixture decreases as the temperature is raised, from a high value at 300 K to a much lower value at 500 K.

questions.solution_md: K falls with T: exothermic; percentage of B falls.

marking_scheme.step: Forward reaction exothermic, by Le Chatelier

questions.stem_md:
Nitrogen dioxide forms in $\ce{2NO(g) + O2(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$, $\Delta H = -114$ kJ, in a closed vessel.

(a) State Le Chatelier's principle. [1]

(b) Predict, with reasons, the effect on the amount of $\ce{NO2}$ at equilibrium of lowering the temperature, increasing the pressure and adding a catalyst. [2]

(c) Helium is added to the equilibrium mixture. What happens to the amount of $\ce{NO2}$ (i) at constant volume and (ii) at constant total pressure? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change of concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that tends to reduce (oppose) the change.

(b) Lower temperature: the forward reaction is exothermic, so it is favoured; NO₂ increases (K increases). Higher pressure: 3 mol of gas → 2 mol, so the forward reaction is favoured; NO₂ increases. Catalyst: no effect on the amount at equilibrium (it speeds up both reactions equally); equilibrium is reached sooner.

(c) (i) At constant volume the concentrations do not change, so there is no shift and the amount of NO₂ is unchanged. (ii) At constant pressure the volume increases and the concentrations fall; the equilibrium shifts to the side with more moles of gas (towards NO and O₂), so the amount of NO₂ decreases.

questions.solution_md: Principle stated; lower T and higher P increase NO₂, catalyst none; helium: no change at constant V, decrease at constant P.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Lower temperature and higher pressure both increase NO₂, with reasons
(b) Catalyst: no change in the amount
(c)(ii) Shift towards NO and O₂ at constant pressure

questions.stem_md: The conditions that give a good rate and a satisfactory yield of ammonia in the Haber process are:

options.text_md: about 200 atm, about 700–720 K, and finely divided iron with a molybdenum promoter
about 1 atm, about 300 K, and finely divided iron with a molybdenum promoter
about 200 atm, about 300 K, and platinum gauze
about 1 atm, about 700–720 K, and vanadium(V) oxide

questions.solution_md: High pressure favours NH₃ (4 mol → 2 mol of gas); about 700–720 K is a compromise between yield (exothermic) and rate; iron with Mo as promoter is the catalyst — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the contact process, $\ce{2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g)}$ ($\Delta H = -196$ kJ) is carried out at only about 1–2 atm, although high pressure would favour the product. This is because:

options.text_md: high pressure would shift the equilibrium towards SO₂ and O₂
a high conversion is already obtained at this pressure, and high pressure would add cost and corrosion without much gain
the catalyst works only at low pressure
low pressure increases the value of the equilibrium constant

questions.solution_md: The forward reaction reduces the number of gas moles, so pressure does favour SO₃, but the equilibrium conversion is already high at about 1–2 atm, so costly high-pressure plant is not justified — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A laboratory prepares ethyl ethanoate from ethanoic acid and ethanol, $\ce{CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O}$. The maximum yield of ester is obtained by:

options.text_md: using an excess of ethanol and adding concentrated sulphuric acid, which removes water and acts as a catalyst
using an excess of water and dilute sulphuric acid as catalyst
raising the pressure of the mixture to 200 atm
using equal amounts of the reactants and adding a catalyst of iron

questions.solution_md: Excess reactant and removal of a product (water, taken up by conc. H₂SO₄) shift the equilibrium forward. The reaction has Δn_g = 0 and takes place in the liquid phase, so pressure has no effect — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The yield of $\ce{NO2}$ from $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$, $\Delta H = +57.2$ kJ, is greatest at high temperature and low pressure.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The forward reaction is endothermic (favoured by high temperature) and increases the number of moles of gas (favoured by low pressure).

questions.stem_md: In the Haber process the gases leaving the reactor are cooled so that ammonia liquefies and is taken out, and the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled. Why is this done?

answer.model_answer_md: Ammonia liquefies at a much higher temperature than nitrogen and hydrogen, so cooling removes it. Removing the product lowers its concentration and shifts the equilibrium forward (Le Chatelier), so more ammonia can form from the recycled gases, and the overall conversion is high.

questions.solution_md: Removing NH₃ shifts equilibrium forward; recycling raises overall conversion.

marking_scheme.step: Shift forward by Le Chatelier; recycling gives high overall yield

questions.stem_md: State the temperature and pressure conditions that give the maximum dissociation of $\ce{N2O4}$ into $\ce{NO2}$ and justify them.

answer.model_answer_md: High temperature, because the dissociation N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is endothermic (ΔH = +57.2 kJ), and low pressure, because the dissociation increases the number of moles of gas from 1 to 2.

questions.solution_md: High temperature (endothermic) and low pressure (more gas moles).

questions.stem_md: Justify the choice of temperature, pressure and catalyst in the conversion of $\ce{SO2}$ to $\ce{SO3}$ in the contact process, $\ce{2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g)}$, $\Delta H = -196$ kJ.

answer.model_answer_md: Temperature about 720–725 K: the reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield, but too low a temperature makes the reaction too slow; this is the compromise. Pressure about 1–2 atm: the forward reaction reduces the moles of gas, so pressure favours SO₃, but the conversion is already high near atmospheric pressure, so high pressure is not needed. Catalyst: vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅, speeds up the approach to equilibrium without changing the equilibrium yield.

questions.solution_md: About 720 K (compromise), 1–2 atm (high conversion already), V₂O₅ catalyst.

marking_scheme.step: Temperature: exothermic reaction, compromise with rate
V₂O₅ catalyst speeds up the rate only

questions.stem_md: Explain why very low temperatures are not used in the manufacture of ammonia although the reaction is exothermic, and name the catalyst that makes the chosen temperature workable.

answer.model_answer_md: Low temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield of ammonia because the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is exothermic (ΔH = −92.4 kJ), but the rate becomes far too slow to be useful, since few molecules have the activation energy. A moderately high temperature, about 700–720 K, gives an acceptable rate, and finely divided iron with molybdenum as promoter is used to increase the rate further without a higher temperature. The poorer yield at this temperature is offset by a pressure of about 200 atm and by removing ammonia and recycling the gases.

questions.solution_md: Rate too slow at low T; compromise about 700 K; Fe with Mo catalyst; 200 atm offsets the yield.

marking_scheme.step: Low T gives better yield but too slow a rate
Compromise temperature with iron and molybdenum catalyst
High pressure and recycling offset the lower yield

questions.stem_md:
Ammonia is made by $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}$, $\Delta H = -92.4$ kJ.

(a) Write the expression for $K_p$ and state its unit. [1]

(b) Using Le Chatelier's principle, state the effect of temperature and of pressure on the equilibrium yield. [2]

(c) State the conditions used in industry and explain how they give a good yield at a good rate. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{NH}_3}^2}{p_{\text{N}_2}\,p_{\text{H}_2}^3}$, unit atm⁻².

(b) The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature gives a higher yield (K increases). It reduces the moles of gas (4 → 2), so a higher pressure gives a higher yield.

(c) About 200 atm and about 700–720 K, with finely divided iron and a molybdenum promoter; the unreacted gases are recycled and ammonia is liquefied and removed. A very low temperature would be too slow, so a moderate temperature is a compromise and the catalyst gives a useful rate; the high pressure raises the yield; removing ammonia shifts the equilibrium forward.

questions.solution_md: Kp = p(NH₃)² / (p(N₂)p(H₂)³), atm⁻²; low T and high P favour yield; industry uses about 200 atm and 700 K with Fe-Mo.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Low temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction
(b) High pressure favours fewer moles of gas
(c) Conditions: about 200 atm, about 700 K, Fe with Mo
(c) Compromise explained; ammonia removal and recycling

questions.stem_md:
Ethyl ethanoate is made from, and hydrolysed back to, ethanoic acid and ethanol: $\ce{CH3COOC2H5 + H2O <=> CH3COOH + C2H5OH}$.

(a) Write the expression for $K_c$ for the hydrolysis (reverse of esterification). [1]

(b) State two ways of increasing the yield of ester in the esterification, with reasons. [2]

(c) State two ways of increasing the yield of ethanoic acid in the hydrolysis, and explain why changing the pressure has no effect on either reaction. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $K_c = \dfrac{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}][\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}$.

(b) Use an excess of one reactant (ethanol), which shifts the equilibrium forward; remove water with concentrated sulphuric acid, or distil off the ester as it forms, so that the equilibrium shifts forward.

(c) Use a large excess of water, and remove ethanoic acid or ethanol as it forms (with dilute acid as catalyst to reach equilibrium sooner). Pressure has no effect because the reaction is in the liquid phase and the number of moles of gas does not change (Δn_g = 0).

questions.solution_md: K_c for hydrolysis; excess reactant and removal of product; excess water; no pressure effect (liquid phase, Δn_g = 0).

marking_scheme.step: (b) Removal of water or ester with reason
(c) Excess water or removal of a product
